Law School Admission Council 662 Penn Street, Newtown PA 18940-0040 LSAC P: 215.504.1466 Email: registrar@lsac.org Dear Colleague: This Law School Report includes a transcript of the candidate's enrollment during Spring 2020 and/or subsequent semesters during which the COVID-19 pandemic affected students' education. The COVID-19 pandemic emerged in early 2020, and the response of many higher education institutions was to convert mid- semester to online education and to announce changes in their traditional grading systems. During Spring 2020, Fall 2020 and subsequent semesters, many students were faced with unanticipated changes in the circumstances of their enrollment. During Spring 2020, students on residential campuses were in many cases required to leave campus with little advance notice; students on spring break were instructed not to return to campus. Many international students either could not leave campus or could not return to their home countries. As the Fall 2020 semester began, schools that may have planned for in-person classes were forced to pivot to online or hybrid classes with very little notice to students. The disruption to students' lives from the rapid change in their physical and learning environments may have included effects on physical or mental health, financial security, and access to academic resources and support services. Notably, many colleges and universities changed their grading systems. Some converted to a mandatory Pass/Fail (or similar) system, others permitted students to choose whether to receive traditional or Pass/Fail grades, still others retained their traditional grading systems. This letter is included in the Law School report as a reminder of the unusual and difficult circumstances surrounding enrollment during the period of time when the COVID-19 pandemic presented a barrier to traditional learning. Law school admission staff may wish to take these circumstances into account. Sincerely, LSAC Credential Processing LSAC.org

LSAC Candidate Name: Ariana Arvanitis Candidate ID: 45090489 Date: 2025-04-21 Prompt ID: WPBA018-01 Writing Prompt Single-Use Plastic Bans Plastic pollution creates environmental hazards and health problems for humans and animals alike, particularly in ocean ecosystems, where wildlife feeding patterns and activity are affected. Single-use plastic products like shopping bags and drinking straws are of special concern because they're intentionally designed to be used once and then thrown away- hence the use of the term "disposable." On the other hand, proponents of these products argue that they have become an indispensable cornerstone of the modern economy because of their practical utility. They also point out that the alternatives to single-use plastics, like cloth shopping bags, often have a greater overall environmental impact. Nevertheless, to address plastic pollution, many countries, including Canada, China, India, Mali, and Rwanda, have banned single-use plastic products. KEY QUESTION: Should governments ban single-use plastic products? Read and carefully consider the arguments presented in the following perspectives. Each suggests a particular way of thinking about the issue captured in the Key Question. Perspective 1 - an excerpt from a newsletter devoted to environmental activism Besides polluting the environment, plastic bags also harm the economy, use up natural resources, and pose health risks to humans. Society pays to unclog waterways jammed with plastic bags and to clean up plastic litter, using public funds that could be better spent on providing other important social services. Moreover, since plastic bags are made of petroleum, they waste precious oil resources. Finally, since plastic breaks down into microplastics that end up in our food and drinking water, it poses health risks to humans, especially the more than 3 billion people dependent on food from the sea. Granted, enforcing single-use plastic bans is difficult, but where they are actively enforced, they have proven effective. For example, one jurisdiction in India strictly enforced its ban, fining some retailers repeatedly for using throwaway bags and allowing the public to report violators on an app. Now, most streets in this jurisdiction of 80 million people are free of plastic waste. Similarly, Rwanda's ban met with success after that country levied the equivalent of a $150 fine on anyone carrying a plastic bag. Perspective 2 - an excerpt from an article in a business journal Though policy debates focus primarily on the questions of practicality and effectiveness, it is equally important to evaluate the ethics of any government policy before it is implemented. In particular, government policies should not violate citizens' personal freedoms or overstep the government's proper role. Plastic bag bans interfere with the consumer's freedom and best judgment, which are important components of a functioning free market. It's not the government's role to dictate what products a citizen can use. Plastic bag bans represent government overreach into private decisions.

From a more practical perspective, much consumer buying activity happens on impulse. Plastic bags facilitate convenient shopping and therefore increased consumer spending. Banning plastic bags in favor of reusable alternatives would slow down consumer spending by forcing shoppers to plan ahead, and in so doing, would hurt the economy. Perspective 3 - an excerpt from a report on global recycling policies The impact of any public policy must be considered in order to justify its implementation. After California banned single- use plastic bags, retailers began offering reusable, heavy-duty plastic bags instead. But many customers didn't actually reuse them because they too closely resembled the single-use disposable bags. And almost none were recycled. So, unfortunately, the local recycling agency reported that people there threw away more plastic bags, by weight, than before the law passed. This tells us that a ban on single-use plastics is unlikely to succeed without being rooted in strong social norms. Even good solutions can't succeed without public support. Moreover, regulations often dilute the individual's sense of personal responsibility to engage in good citizenship. Therefore, instead of bans, littering and pollution should be addressed through education and civic engagement. Voluntary initiatives would also reduce the government's costs for enforcing a ban. Chile, Finland, France, and Indonesia have all achieved reduced plastic bag waste through voluntary initiatives. For instance, France reported a decrease in single-use plastic bag use from 10.5 billion in 2002 to 800 million in 2013 through voluntary initiatives that focused on promoting reusable shopping bags made from other materials. Perspective 4 - an excerpt from a plastics industry newsletter Perhaps the first test of sound public policy should be the one we use for sound medical policy: Do no harm! Sadly, banning plastics would do harm, since plastic substitutes are usually worse, in two ways. First, plastic substitutes are typically less environmentally friendly. For instance, although paper bags easily biodegrade, they consume more energy to produce than plastic bags do. Similarly, reusable cloth bags require more than 100 uses to justify the extra energy required to produce them. Due to the additional energy expended in manufacturing, distributing, and disposing of them, reusable bags cause even greater environmental damage than single-use plastics do: to the soil from oil production, to the air from pollutants and greenhouse gases, to the water from polluted runoff, and to the landscape by going back into landfills. Second, plastic substitutes can have unanticipated health impacts. Researchers have found that reusable bags can carry bacteria and viruses that can infect us through our groceries unless the bags are washed periodically, which most people don't do. Prewriting Analysis: Generating Ideas for Your Argumentative Essay Spend the remainder of your prewriting time working through the prewriting questions presented below. These questions are intended to help you think critically about the issue and generate productive ideas for your essay. Record your thoughts in your digital scratch paper by making notes or lists, or by writing short answers to the questions. Your notes in response to the prewriting questions will still be available to you while you write your essay, but they will not be evaluated or included as part of your essay. These questions are strictly provided to help guide your analysis of the perspectives and to help you develop your own argument in response to the Key Question. Prewriting Questions Which perspective(s) do you find most compelling? What relevant insights do you see in the perspective(s)? What principles or values do you see at work in the perspective(s)? What strengths and weaknesses can you find in the perspective(s)? Your argument should incorporate or address ideas from at least one of the perspectives provided. In addition, your own knowledge, experiences, and personal values can be valid sources of evidence, and you can include these in your essay: What knowledge do you already have about this issue? Consider information you have read or heard, including things you've learned at home or school, etc. What values influence your position on this issue? Consider your worldview or belief system, as well as any guiding principles or convictions you hold. What experiences do you have that might be relevant to this issue? Consider any personal experience you might have with this or similar issues, or other relevant lessons learned from your own life.

Response: Growing up in Miami, Florida, a city nestled between dense swamps and pristine beaches, I was taught from an early age that it was my utmost responsibility to be a steward of the earth and protect the fragile ecosystems that surrounded my home city. Between field trips to Everglades National Park and weekends spent on the Key Biscayne beaches, I witnessed exactly how single-use plastics can find themselves in the wrong places, whether that be entangled in the roots of a mangrove or floating around aimlessly under a dock. There is no doubt that plastic pollution is a problem that we as a global society are facing together. However, the solution to single-use plastics polluting the environment may not be as simple as it seems. Although tempting to suggest an outright ban of single-use plastics, the potential ramifications indicate that a ban may be more harmful than it would be beneficial. Thus, governments should not ban single-use plastics due to lack of social norms that inhibit follow through, the proven effectiveness of volunteer initiatives in other countries, and the negative impact on the free market. According to Perspective 3, a significant reason as to why single-use plastics should not be banned stems from an instance in which the state of California banned single-use plastics, but it did not result in a positive impact on the environment. Customers did not reuse the reusable, heavy-duty plastic bags that meant to replace single-use plastic bags, which thus resulted in a greater amount of trash as measured by weight. The root of this predicament was found to be that there is not a strong culture or set social norm to guide society's attitude toward single-use plastics. Public support is a critical component of any policy implementation as it helps to ensure that people will follow through once a new initiative is set in place. However, California serves as an important example as to how society would react if governments enacted a ban of single-use plastics. If in California, a state traditionally known for its protection of the great outdoors, there is not a powerful social norm to compel people to reuse heavy-duty plastic bags, this social norm, or lack thereof, is likely to be entirely absent from other parts of the country. This would render a ban to be entirely ineffective. Another reason as to why governments should not enforce a ban of single-use plastics is due to the success of volunteer initiatives in other countries such as Chile, Finland, France, and Indonesia. As mentioned in Perspective 3, it appears as though there is not an existing social norm to encourage people to adopt a new approach to reusing heavy-duty plastic bags. However, when the aim of reducing single-use plastics from the environment is communicated to the public through education and civic engagement, success seems to be much more likely. Perspective 3 notes that in France, voluntary initiatives resulted in the decrease of single- use plastic bags from 10.5 billion in 2002 to 800 million in 2013. This was primarily facilitated through the promotion of shopping bags made from more sustainable and reusable materials. When people volunteer to cooperate for a global cause they are passionate about, they seem to be much more open to committing to the use of products that help make the mission of the cause feel much more attainable. According to Perspective 2, an additional reason that the ban of single-use plastic bags would not be beneficial to the environment is that a large portion of buying activity is spontaneous and encouraged due to single-use plastics. For example, if someone just purchased a new book and it is now raining outside, a plastic bag would serve as an excellent cover for that book and ensure that it does not get wet upon leaving the bookstore. However, if the plastic bag was not an option upon checking out of the store, consumers may be more inclined to refrain from making a purchase since they may believe that the product they just purchased is bound to be destroyed by the rain. Thus, an impromptu purchase at the bookstore could very well be impacted by the lack of availability of single-use plastics. Perspective 2 argues that these small, impulsive purchases overall contribute greatly to the economy and if they ceased there would be grand economic consequences. When economic turmoil is on the horizon, people tend to focus on the economy rather than the other issues we as a global society face. Thus, attention may be taken away from existing environmental efforts, which puts solving environmental issues toward the bottom of the agenda and slows progress and other current efforts being made. One common argument against the ban of single-use plastics may be that there are other countries that have successfully banned them. According to Perspective 1, India and Rwanda have introduced bans that have proven to be effective. However, the circumstances in India and Rwanda are very different than they are in other countries. For example, the California ban of single-use plastic bags demonstrates that a ban across the entire United States would likely fail. Additionally, India appears to have the technological infrastructure to report violators who are in possession of single-use plastics on an app. Not only does that app not exist in the

United States, for example, but allowing American citizens to quickly report each other for not adhering to the ban would likely trespass on the freedom consumers are entitled to as outlined in Perspective 2. Perspective 2 advocates that governments should not dictate which products people use because it would then be deviating from its proper role. Allowing other citizens to enforce the government's policies on each other through an app seems as though it would not allow people to act freely. Ultimately, a ban on single-use plastics would do more harm to society than good. Lack of public support and social norms, the effectiveness of volunteer initiatives, and the potentially negative impact on the economy are all significant reasons to steer away from a ban. If in the future we are to ensure that as little plastic as possible is roaming around the wild and is secure in designated places for garbage and recycling processing, it seems as though governments ought to begin with a volunteer initiative that will stimulate public support. With a strong foundation of public support, only then should governments re-evaluate the idea of a ban and see if it suits the earth's needs at that moment.

THE UNIVERSITY OF College of Liberal Arts & Sciences KU KANSAS Communication Studies Dear Admissions Committee, I am writing to recommend Ariana Arvanitis for entry into law school. In my role as debate coach for Carrollton School of the Sacred Heart in Miami, FL, I have had the pleasure of overseeing and evaluating Ari over the last three years in her capacity as an Assistant Debate Coach, mentor of young students, and adjudicator of debate rounds. Carrollton is the only all-girl nationally competitive policy debate program in the country, and Ari has had a significant hand in the success of the program. I coached Ari through four high school debate seasons. As a debater, she was excellent and successful yet remained humble as she won with grace. During her college years, Ari worked informally with the program, before taking on a more significant role after her graduation from Tufts. As Ari's coach first, and then subsequently her employer, I have a dual perspective that provides me with a comprehensive understanding of her intellectual prowess, character, and leadership. Debate success requires rapidly assimilating complex material from a variety of disciplines and transforming that material into persuasive arguments. Ari took the skills she developed as a debater and became an even better coach. She consistently demonstrated the ability to complete difficult research, spot logical fallacies in opposing arguments, and reframe complex issues into accessible, compelling cases. For example, in one coaching session Ari discussed the relationship between legal positivism and critical legal studies, and in the next Ari provided students with the tools to explain how trademark law could be used to prevent imported counterfeits. Ari became our "go-to" coach at taking convoluted arguments and teaching young women, who commonly spoke English as a second language, how to take on the best and brightest from around the country. In addition to her role as a debate coach and teacher to her own students, Ari judged dozens of debates involving high school students from other schools. In policy debate, teams get to rank their judges, and Ari was consistently ranked highly--finding herself in some of the best, and most difficult to decide, debates at every tournament she attended. She was ranked highly because coaches trusted her to fairly evaluate the arguments in front of her and provide meaningful feedback to the debaters after the debate had concluded. Maggie Bertheume, the Director of Debate at Woodward Academy in Atlanta, confirmed Woodward's desire to have Ari judge her students, noting that Ari was "fair, thoughtful, and well-reasoned, and always gave excellent feedback to the students." LSAT Score Information All LSAT tests are valid and reliable predictors of law school success because they are all composed of questions from the same banks, and all questions are continuously reviewed by experts to ensure quality, reliability, and validity. All test sections include approximately the same number of questions and cover the same content areas of analytical reasoning, logical reasoning, and reading comprehension. The score scale is 120-180 for all tests. The LSAT (including the LSAT-Flex) is the only test specifically designed to predict first-year performance in law school. The LSAT is supported by decades of empirical evidence verifying its efficacy in predicting first-year law school performance by testing skills rated by law professors as most important to classroom success. Percentiles provided with all scores are based on the previous three-year period. LSAT (5 sections), June 1991 to May 2020 The LSAT using the current 120-180 scale was administered from June 1991 through April 2020, and it consisted of four scored sections and one unscored section. Tests were administered in person at test centers. All scores earned during this period will be averaged together. (Earlier versions of the LSAT, using a different score scale, were offered between 1948 and 1991.) LSAT-Flex, May 2020 through July 2021 The LSAT-Flex was administered from May 2020 through July 2021, and it consisted of three scored sections and no unscored section. The LSAT-Flex was designed in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. Tests were administered online with live remote proctoring. Scores on the LSAT-Flex will be averaged with other LSAT-Flex scores and with the four-section LSAT described below beginning in August 2021.
